These differences indicate that vaccination opportunity is structured not only by eligibil­ ity definition but also by where women access care at dif­ ferent stages of pregnancy.

The interaction between eligibility window and care patterns by level of care has operational implications. Under the narrower 24–36 week window, eligibility is more sensitive to the timing of individual visits, par­ ticularly at facilities where women are seen later or less frequently. The broader ≥ 28 week definition increases the likelihood that a routine contact will coincide with vaccine eligibility across levels of care. Daily atten­ dance volumes further shape feasibility. Tertiary hospi­ tals consistently recorded the highest daily volumes of vaccine-eligible women. This finding was anticipated, as secondary facilities are more commonly accessed for episodic or acute services, whereas hospitals represent a subsequent and more consistent site for providing ANC, as reflected in both national data and our findings [22]. Applying the ≥ 28 week definition increased these daily volumes by 1 visits per day in secondary facilities and 5–9 visits per day in tertiary facilities, reflecting both broader eligibility and larger overall patient loads at the tertiary level. Adoption of a broader eligibility window would therefore expand potential reach while simultaneously increasing the number of women eligible for vaccination at high-volume sites, requiring corresponding adjust­ ments in vaccine supply, staffing, and workflow planning. Lower-volume facilities may require different microplan­ ning approaches tailored to predictable but smaller num­ bers of eligible women.

Operational feasibility also differs structurally across levels of care. At the primary level of care we found rou­ tine ANC visits occur more frequently than at higher levels of care, though daily vaccine-eligible volumes could not be quantified for this level. Existing evidence from Viet Nam highlights persistent infrastructure and workforce constraints at primary-level facilities, includ­ ing limited on-site cold-chain capacity, small health care teams, and reliance on coordinated supply delivery from higher-level facilities [23, 24]. These constraints have direct implications for the feasibility of same-day maternal RSV vaccination, particularly in ensuring reli­ able vaccine availability and adequate time for counsel­ ing during routine ANC visits. Hospitals may have more existing resources to support on-site storage, accommo­ date higher staffing needs, and integrated service deliv­ ery, which may facilitate vaccination during eligible visits at scale. Maternal RSV vaccination planning must there­ fore be tailored to the level of care: the number of eligi­ ble women, timing of contacts, and operational capacity

differ across levels of care, and uniform delivery strate­ gies may not be appropriate.

Differences across sectors further extend this argu­ ment. In an ad hoc comparison of the two tertiary care facilities included in this study—one private and one public—women attending the private facility had an ear­ lier median GA at first recorded visit (median 25 weeks) and more documented visits (median two visits) than those attending the public facility, where first recorded visits occurred later and were fewer in number (median 37 weeks at first recorded visit, median one visit total). Although limited to two sites, these observations are consistent with documented differences in care-seeking pathways between public and private sectors in Viet Nam [22] and is relevant for consideration in maternal RSV vaccination planning.

These sectoral differences have direct implications for how vaccine eligibility policy translates into access. Ear­ lier presentation at private tertiary facilities could facili­ tate maternal RSV vaccine delivery under narrower GA eligibility windows, while later presentation at public facilities could limit access without broader eligibility criteria or adaptations to current delivery strategies. In this context, eligibility definitions interact not only with level of care but also with sector-specific care patterns, potentially shaping who is reached during early phases of vaccine introduction. This has important implications for broader rollout strategy and equity. Targeted outreach and education will likely be needed to reach women seeking care in the public sector, alongside coordinated delivery strategies that account for movement between sectors.

These findings highlight the need for coordinated maternal RSV vaccination strategies that account for care-seeking across the full range of facility levels and types. Primary level facilities are often the first point of contact in pregnancy, making them a critical setting for early education and demand generation for maternal RSV vaccination. Although many women initially present within the first trimester, primary care facilities also con­ tinue to see women later in pregnancy when they would be eligible to receive the vaccine. In contrast, higher-level facilities tend to see women later in pregnancy and often only once, generally within the vaccination eligibility period. As a result, these facilities must prioritize readi­ ness for same-day vaccination to avoid missed opportu­ nities. Across all levels of care, linked health records are essential to ensure continuity: integrated systems help prevent inadvertent revaccination while also ensuring that women are not missed for vaccination as they move between facilities and levels of the health system.

Given that Viet Nam has not yet rolled out the mater­ nal RSV vaccine in the public sector, these data provide timely evidence to inform policy decisions. Revisiting

the eligibility window for maternal RSV vaccination from the current 24- to 36-weeks’ GA to the third trimester (≥ 28-week GA) could substantially increase coverage and protect more infants. Optimizing maternal RSV cover­ age will require adapting education and service delivery strategies to the realities of care-seeking behavior and ensuring robust health information systems that support continuity of care across all facility types and sectors.

One strength of this study is the use of real-world ANC register data from diverse facility levels, capturing patient and provider practices rather than relying on modeled estimates. Collecting data after the peak of COVID-19 service disruptions and excluding clinic closure days allowed for realistic estimates of ANC service volumes. Data completeness was also high; GA was available for every ANC visit recorded in the study period in all study facilities.

Our study has several limitations. The absence of unique patient identifiers in ANC registers made it impossible to track women across health facilities. As in most countries, the tiered maternal health system in Viet Nam accommodates women seeking care at mul­ tiple facilities during a single pregnancy. Consequently, facility-based records may reflect episodic service con­ tacts rather than individual care pathways, resulting in estimates that reflect patterns of service utilization at the facility level rather than individual-level timing of care initiation and follow up. Also, due to changing elec­ tronic register ownership and record accessibility, data from tertiary facilities were restricted to a single calen­ dar year, 2023, while lower-levels of care included data from 2022 to 2024, thus limiting the direct comparabil­ ity of ANC timing patterns between levels of care. While we addressed within-facility selection bias through ran­ dom sampling at facilities with paper-based records and included all women at facilities with electronic registers, the overall data overrepresents women attending tertiary care, who may differ systematically from women at lower levels of care. Finally, by including only women with documented ANC visits, our findings may overestimate potential RSV vaccine coverage at the population level.

Conclusions This research underscores the importance of aligning maternal RSV immunization strategies with ANC atten­ dance patterns across levels of the health system in Viet Nam. Timing and frequency of ANC visits play a cen­ tral role in shaping vaccine opportunity, and observed differences by level of care highlight the need for tar­ geted delivery strategies. Focusing vaccination counsel­ ing and education efforts on primary facilities will be particularly important in Viet Nam because these set­ tings consistently demonstrate earlier and more regu­ lar engagement of women attending ANC. Aligning

national GA eligibility guidance with observed ANC attendance, particularly adoption of the WHO-recom­ mended ≥ 28-week eligibility window, could substantially expand opportunities for RSV vaccination within existing service delivery platforms. Achieving high and equitable coverage will require translating these opportunities into practice through strengthening early ANC engagement and counseling, tailored scheduling and logistics based on facility-level attendance patterns, and expansion of access beyond the private sector to public facilities. Investment in integrated digital health information sys­ tems that support the continuity of ANC records across facilities would further strengthen program planning and help ensure women have opportunities to receive mater­ nal RSV vaccination regardless of where care is sought. Collectively, these actions can support effective, efficient, and equitable national rollout of maternal RSV vaccine in Viet Nam.
